name: Montana
one: In Montana, ask for your ballot by Monday, November 2, 2026.In Montana, the last day to ask for a mail ballot was Monday, November 2, 2026: you can still vote in person, early or on Election Day.
sec:
Vote by mail or absentee

Can’t get to your polling place on Election Day? Here is how to vote by mail in Montana, from the state’s own election office and its laws. Checked October 21, 2026.

Ask for your ballot by

Monday, November 2Passed

Your request must be made before noon on Monday, November 2, 2026 (the law says before noon on the day before the election). If you become sick or have a health emergency after 5 p.m. on Friday, October 30, you can still ask your county to bring you a ballot, up to the close of polls on Election Day. (the law)

Send it back by

Tuesday, November 3Passed

Your ballot must be received by 8 p.m. on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3, 2026. A postmark is not enough. The Secretary of State suggests mailing it at least one week before Election Day (by Tuesday, October 27, 2026). (the law)

The last day to ask for a ballot by mail has passed. You can still vote in person, early or on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3. When and where to vote early.

Montana’s own page on voting by mail

At school away from home, in Montana or in another state? What Montana says about students is under Show more.

Who can vote by mail

No reason is needed. State law says any registered voter may vote by absentee ballot. (the law)

How to ask for a ballot

  • By mail. Fill in the state's absentee ballot application, or write your own request that gives your birth date and is signed by you, and send it to the election administrator of the county where you live. The application is on the Secretary of State's election forms page. Montana has no online request form. Open it (the law)
  • In person. Once ballots are ready, you can go to your county election administrator's office, ask for an absentee ballot, and mark it there. (the law)
  • For every election. You can ask to be put on the absentee ballot list, so a ballot is mailed to you for every election while you stay at the same address. The county mails a form in January of each even-numbered year to voters the Postal Service lists as having moved; if you do not answer it, you are taken off the list. (the law)

How to send it back

  • By mail. Mail it back in the signature envelope, with postage (the law says "postage paid"; check your envelope). It must arrive by 8 p.m. on Election Day, so mail it at least a week ahead. (the law)
  • In person. Drop it off at your county election office, or at any polling place in your county, by 8 p.m. on Election Day. (the law)

What the envelope needs

No witness or notary is needed. Put your marked ballot in the secrecy envelope, put that in the signature envelope, then sign the statement printed on the signature envelope. State law also asks for your date of birth on the envelope; the Secretary of State's page asks you to sign, date and write your birth year, and says the birth year rule is "not currently enforced". If you registered without showing ID, you may also put a copy of a photo ID or a document such as a utility bill or bank statement with your name and address in the outer envelope. (the law)

Track your ballot

Track your ballot on Montana’s own site (official page)

Vote early in person instead

You can vote an absentee ballot in person at your county election administrator's office once ballots are ready, 30 days before the election (Sunday, October 4, 2026, so in practice from the office's first open day after that). Ballots were mailed to absentee voters starting Friday, October 9, 2026. The state's calendar lists election offices open on Saturday, October 31, 2026, from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., and says a court order has blocked the wider Saturday registration and voting that a new law (Senate Bill 490) would have added; ask your county what it offers that day. (the law)

Students

At school in Montana, away from home

The Secretary of State's pages we could read do not speak to students separately. State law says you do not gain a new home in a Montana county by moving there for a temporary purpose such as an educational program, unless you mean to make that county your permanent home after the program ends. Your home is where you live and mean to return to when you are away. A student registered at a home address elsewhere in Montana can ask that county for an absentee ballot and give a different mailing address. (the law)

At school in another state, with Montana as home

State law says you do not lose your Montana home by going to another state for a temporary purpose, meaning to return, unless you vote in that other state. If you move to another state meaning to live there, you lose your Montana residence. A student who keeps Montana as home can request a Montana absentee ballot from their county. (the law)

Military and overseas

Members of the military, their families, and citizens living overseas get their ballot at least 45 days before the election. A ballot counts if it is received by 8 p.m. on Election Day, or by 5 p.m. on the day after (Wednesday, November 4, 2026) if it was sent electronically by 8 p.m. on Election Day. A federal write-in absentee ballot must be sent by 8 p.m. on Election Day and received by 3 p.m. on the following Monday (November 9, 2026). The Federal Voting Assistance Program explains the federal forms. (the law)

Montana in the Federal Voting Assistance Program’s guide

Good to know

  • Montana requires the ballot to be in hand by 8 p.m. on Election Day, not just postmarked. With less than two weeks left, a ballot requested by mail now may not make the round trip in time; you can request, mark and hand in a ballot at your county election office instead.
  • Late registration covers the 30 days before the election (it began October 6, 2026); a voter who registers late must get their ballot in person from the county election office.
  • The federal write-in absentee ballot deadline (sent by 8 p.m. on Election Day, received by 3 p.m. the following Monday) is in state law 13-21-206 (source 11).
  • The Saturday, October 31 office hours and the court order come from the Secretary of State's 2026 calendar (source 9).

How this was checked

  • The Secretary of State's main site (sosmt.gov) answered our request with a check for human visitors, so its absentee and military pages were not read; the facts here come from VoteMT.gov (also run by the Secretary of State) and from state law. The forms page link is given but was not read.
  • The FVAP page loads by script and could not be read; it is linked, not quoted. Military and overseas facts here come from state law.

polls:
Polls are open 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. (small polling places from noon). (the law)

Anyone in line when the polls close may still vote.
